topics.title: Chapter 7 — Processes and Resource Management
topics.summary: A server feels slow, and the first visible process uses a large amount of memory. Killing it seems decisive, but the process may be the database doing legitimate work while the real problem is a saturated storage path. Resource management requires identifying what is running, what it is waiting for, and which limit actually constrains the workload.

blocks.text: A server feels slow, and the first visible process uses a large amount of memory. Killing it seems decisive, but the process may be the database doing legitimate work while the real problem is a saturated storage path. Resource management requires identifying what is running, what it is waiting for, and which limit actually constrains the workload.

This chapter distinguishes process identity, scheduling, memory accounting, signals, and resource boundaries. Observation comes before termination. A process is part of a service lifecycle, not merely a row to remove from a screen.

topics.title: 7.1 Programs vs. Processes
topics.summary: A program is executable code stored or otherwise available for execution. A process is a running instance with its own identity, address space, open file descriptors, credentials, and execution state. Many processes can run the same program with different arguments and permissions.

concepts.definition: A program is executable code stored or otherwise available for execution. A process is a running instance with its own identity, address space, open file descriptors, credentials, and execution state. Many processes can run the same program with different arguments and permissions.

cards.question: Explain 7.1 Programs vs. Processes. What does the source establish?

cards.question: What should you check after this section’s example?
cards.answer: The file is a program; the shell PID identifies a process executing it.

blocks.text: A program is executable code stored or otherwise available for execution. A process is a running instance with its own identity, address space, open file descriptors, credentials, and execution state. Many processes can run the same program with different arguments and permissions.

A service may consist of one process, a parent and several workers, or a collection of cooperating programs. Killing one worker may cause the supervisor to replace it immediately. That is not evidence that kill failed; it may be the intended lifecycle policy.

Identify the owning service before acting. The service manager often knows which processes belong together and how to stop them cleanly. Stopping a service through its supervisor is usually safer than guessing which PID represents the whole application.
Linux example — 7.1
Compare the executable name with a running instance.

command -v bash
ps -p "$$" -o pid,comm,args
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: What to check: The file is a program; the shell PID identifies a process executing it.

topics.title: 7.2 Process IDs
topics.summary: A process ID, or PID, identifies a process within a PID namespace. PIDs are reused after processes exit. A number copied from an old incident note is therefore not a durable identity.

concepts.definition: A process ID, or PID, identifies a process within a PID namespace. PIDs are reused after processes exit. A number copied from an old incident note is therefore not a durable identity.

cards.question: Explain 7.2 Process IDs. What does the source establish?
cards.answer: A process ID, or PID, identifies a process within a PID namespace. PIDs are reused after processes exit. A number copied from an old incident note is therefore not a durable identity.

cards.question: What should you check after this section’s example?
cards.answer: A PID identifies an instance and can be reused after that instance exits.

blocks.text: A process ID, or PID, identifies a process within a PID namespace. PIDs are reused after processes exit. A number copied from an old incident note is therefore not a durable identity.
ps -p $$ -o pid,ppid,user,etime,comm
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: $$ expands to the shell’s PID in the usual interactive context. The elapsed time and command help establish which process is actually being inspected.

Before signaling a process, confirm its current executable, owner, start time, and relationship to the service. A separate check followed by a later signal still has a race if the process exits and the PID is reused. Service-manager operations and newer process-handle interfaces can reduce ambiguity. Avoid building critical automation around stale PID files alone.
Linux example — 7.2
Inspect the current process ID.

printf 'Shell PID: %s\n' "$$"
ps -p "$$" -o pid,ppid,user,comm
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: What to check: A PID identifies an instance and can be reused after that instance exits.

topics.title: 7.3 Parent and Child Processes
topics.summary: A process can create child processes. The parent PID, or PPID, records a relationship useful for understanding shells, workers, and supervisors. A child can outlive its original parent and be adopted by an appropriate reaper or subreaper.

concepts.definition: A process can create child processes. The parent PID, or PPID, records a relationship useful for understanding shells, workers, and supervisors. A child can outlive its original parent and be adopted by an appropriate reaper or subreaper.

cards.question: Explain 7.3 Parent and Child Processes. What does the source establish?
cards.answer: A process can create child processes. The parent PID, or PPID, records a relationship useful for understanding shells, workers, and supervisors. A child can outlive its original parent and be adopted by an appropriate reaper or subreaper.

cards.question: What should you check after this section’s example?
cards.answer: The child should show your shell as its parent; wait reaps its completion.

blocks.text: A process can create child processes. The parent PID, or PPID, records a relationship useful for understanding shells, workers, and supervisors. A child can outlive its original parent and be adopted by an appropriate reaper or subreaper.
ps -eo pid,ppid,user,stat,comm --forest
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: The process tree reveals relationships, but it does not by itself describe every service boundary. A service’s control group can include processes whose ancestry has changed.

After a child exits, its parent ordinarily collects its termination status through a wait operation. Failing to do so creates a zombie entry, discussed later. Good process supervision includes starting, signaling, collecting exit status, and deciding whether restart is appropriate.
Linux example — 7.3
Observe a controlled child process.

sleep 10 &
child=$!
ps -p "$child" -o pid,ppid,comm
wait "$child"
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: What to check: The child should show your shell as its parent; wait reaps its completion.

topics.summary: ps reports a snapshot of selected processes. Its option styles have historical differences, so use an explicit format when collecting repeatable evidence.

blocks.text: ps reports a snapshot of selected processes. Its option styles have historical differences, so use an explicit format when collecting repeatable evidence.

ps -eo pid,ppid,user,stat,%cpu,%mem,etime,comm \
  --sort=-%cpu
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: The command sorts by the reported CPU measure and avoids dumping complete arguments that might contain secrets. Add arguments only when needed and handle them as potentially sensitive.

ps CPU percentages are not necessarily the same interval measurement shown by an interactive monitor. Its values often reflect CPU time relative to process lifetime. A recently busy process and a long-running process can therefore look different depending on the tool’s measurement model. State the tool and observation interval when reporting performance. (R14)
Linux example — 7.4
Select useful process columns.
ps -eo pid,ppid,user,%cpu,%mem,stat,comm --sort=-%cpu
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: top repeatedly samples processes and system activity. htop, when installed, offers a different interactive interface with convenient navigation. Both are views of measurements, not automatic diagnoses.

Check whether CPU percentages are normalized per logical CPU or across the whole machine. A multithreaded process can exceed 100% in a per-CPU reporting mode. Use thread views when one process contains several independently busy threads.

topics.title: 7.6 Foreground and Background Jobs
topics.summary: A foreground job interacts with the terminal normally. Appending & starts a command asynchronously and returns the shell prompt. Bash assigns a job number distinct from the operating-system PID.

concepts.definition: A foreground job interacts with the terminal normally. Appending & starts a command asynchronously and returns the shell prompt. Bash assigns a job number distinct from the operating-system PID.

cards.question: Explain 7.6 Foreground and Background Jobs. What does the source establish?
cards.answer: A foreground job interacts with the terminal normally. Appending & starts a command asynchronously and returns the shell prompt. Bash assigns a job number distinct from the operating-system PID.

cards.question: What should you check after this section’s example?
cards.answer: jobs reports this shell's job table, not every host process.

blocks.text: A foreground job interacts with the terminal normally. Appending & starts a command asynchronously and returns the shell prompt. Bash assigns a job number distinct from the operating-system PID.

sleep 60 &
job_pid=$!
jobs -l
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: $! captures the PID associated with the most recent asynchronous command. fg returns a job to the foreground; bg resumes a stopped job in the background. These are shell job-control operations, not service-management commands.

Backgrounding a command does not make it a reliable daemon. It may depend on the session, terminal, environment, or working directory. Use a terminal multiplexer for interactive continuity and a supervisor such as systemd for an actual service with restart and logging requirements.
Linux example — 7.6
Run and wait for a short background job.

sleep 2 &
jobs -l
wait "$!"
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: What to check: jobs reports this shell's job table, not every host process.

topics.title: 7.7 Signals
topics.summary: A signal notifies a process of an event or requests an action. SIGTERM asks for termination and can be handled for cleanup. SIGINT commonly corresponds to an interactive interrupt. SIGHUP has historical terminal meaning and application-specific uses. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught or ignored.

blocks.text: A signal notifies a process of an event or requests an action. SIGTERM asks for termination and can be handled for cleanup. SIGINT commonly corresponds to an interactive interrupt. SIGHUP has historical terminal meaning and application-specific uses. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught or ignored.
Do not assume that SIGHUP always reloads configuration. That is an application convention, not a universal kernel rule. Read the service documentation or use its supported reload interface.

SIGKILL prevents application cleanup and can leave incomplete work. It is a last resort after understanding the impact. It also does not make an uninterruptible kernel wait vanish immediately; delivery takes effect when the process can reach an appropriate point.
Linux example — 7.7
List supported signal names.
kill -l

topics.title: 7.8 kill and pkill
topics.summary: kill sends a signal; its name does not mean every use immediately destroys a process. pkill selects processes by criteria and signals the matches. Selection deserves at least as much care as the signal itself.

cards.question: What should you check after this section’s example?
cards.answer: wait commonly reports a signal-related nonzero status; avoid broad pkill patterns.

blocks.text: kill sends a signal; its name does not mean every use immediately destroys a process. pkill selects processes by criteria and signals the matches. Selection deserves at least as much care as the signal itself.
pgrep -a -u "$USER" -x sleep
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: Inspect a proposed match with pgrep before using a corresponding pkill. Exact-name matching is safer than a broad substring, but still may match multiple legitimate jobs. Never run pkill -f against an unreviewed pattern on a production host.

For the known lab process started in Section 7.6, kill -TERM "$job_pid" targets the captured child. Wait for its completion in the same shell with wait "$job_pid", interpreting the expected signal-related status. Do not reuse the variable later after unrelated work.
Linux example — 7.8
Terminate only the sleep process created here.

sleep 60 &
child=$!
kill -TERM "$child"
wait "$child"
# For an application, inspect before selecting targets:
pgrep -a -x bash

topics.title: 7.9 Process Priorities
topics.summary: Scheduling priority influences how runnable work competes for CPU time. It does not manufacture CPU capacity and does not resolve every performance problem. A process blocked on storage may gain little from a CPU-priority change.

concepts.definition: Scheduling priority influences how runnable work competes for CPU time. It does not manufacture CPU capacity and does not resolve every performance problem. A process blocked on storage may gain little from a CPU-priority change.

blocks.text: Scheduling priority influences how runnable work competes for CPU time. It does not manufacture CPU capacity and does not resolve every performance problem. A process blocked on storage may gain little from a CPU-priority change.

Ordinary Linux scheduling and real-time scheduling have different policies. Raising a process into a real-time class without understanding its behavior can starve important system work. Do not treat real-time priority as a generic performance switch.

Measure the actual bottleneck first. For background maintenance, reducing scheduling preference may be appropriate when it protects interactive service latency. Even then, the job can still compete for memory and I/O, so CPU priority is only one part of resource control.
Linux example — 7.9
Inspect scheduling priority fields.
ps -p "$$" -o pid,ni,pri,comm
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: What to check: NI is the nice adjustment; it is not a CPU quota.

topics.title: 7.10 nice and renice
topics.summary: nice starts a command with an adjusted niceness; renice changes an existing process’s niceness. In the ordinary range, a larger numeric nice value means lower scheduling preference. Negative values increase preference and ordinarily require privilege.

concepts.definition: nice starts a command with an adjusted niceness; renice changes an existing process’s niceness. In the ordinary range, a larger numeric nice value means lower scheduling preference. Negative values increase preference and ordinarily require privilege.

cards.question: What should you check after this section’s example?
cards.answer: The child normally shows NI 10 when the parent started at NI 0.

blocks.text: nice starts a command with an adjusted niceness; renice changes an existing process’s niceness. In the ordinary range, a larger numeric nice value means lower scheduling preference. Negative values increase preference and ordinarily require privilege.
nice -n 10 sha256sum /etc/hosts
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: The small example demonstrates syntax without creating a sustained load. For an existing identified process, inspect its current value before changing it with renice.

Niceness is relative competition, not a hard CPU ceiling. A low-priority job can use an otherwise idle CPU fully. For a service that must not exceed a defined allocation, a control-group quota or another explicit resource limit may be more appropriate.
Linux example — 7.10
Start a low-priority disposable process.

nice -n 10 sleep 2 &
child=$!
ps -p "$child" -o pid,ni,comm
wait "$child"

topics.title: 7.11 CPU Utilization
topics.summary: CPU utilization describes how processor time is being spent. Distinguish user-space work, kernel work, idle time, and other reported categories. A busy CPU can indicate productive work, an inefficient loop, encryption, interrupt load, or many other causes.

blocks.text: CPU utilization describes how processor time is being spent. Distinguish user-space work, kernel work, idle time, and other reported categories. A busy CPU can indicate productive work, an inefficient loop, encryption, interrupt load, or many other causes.

A machine with eight logical CPUs can have one saturated application thread while the overall CPU average remains modest. Conversely, a high aggregate percentage can be acceptable when latency targets are met and the workload is intentionally batch-oriented.

Use interval measurements and thread-level evidence when appropriate. Compare against the service’s throughput and response time. “CPU is 100%” is incomplete until you state which CPU or process, over what interval, and whether useful work is progressing.

Use interval measurements and thread-level evidence when appropriate. Compare against the service’s throughput and response time. “CPU is 100%” is incomplete until you state which CPU or process, over what interval, and whether useful work is progressing.

blocks.text: Linux uses memory for application pages, kernel data, page cache, and other purposes. A low free value is not automatically a problem because cache can often be reclaimed. The available estimate is more useful for understanding memory that can likely support new work without swapping.

Process RSS is resident memory, while VSZ describes virtual address space. Large virtual size does not mean every byte is physically resident. Summing RSS can also double-count shared pages across processes.

Investigate growth over time, reclaim activity, swap traffic, allocation failures, and cgroup limits. A memory leak is a pattern tied to workload and lifetime, not simply the largest process in one snapshot. Chapter 22 develops a more complete measurement sequence.

blocks.text: Linux load averages summarize the number of runnable tasks and tasks in certain uninterruptible waits over approximately one, five, and fifteen minutes. They are not CPU percentages.

A load of four means different things on a one-CPU machine and a sixteen-CPU machine. High load with idle CPU can point toward blocked I/O or other uninterruptible waits rather than a shortage of computation.

Compare the trend across intervals: a short-term value much higher than the long-term value suggests a recent increase. Then inspect task states and resource evidence. Dividing load by CPU count can provide context, but it does not turn the result into a universal health score.

topics.title: 7.14 Zombie Processes
topics.summary: A zombie is a process that has exited but whose termination status has not yet been collected by its parent. It is not continuing to execute application code or holding its former full address space.

concepts.definition: A zombie is a process that has exited but whose termination status has not yet been collected by its parent. It is not continuing to execute application code or holding its former full address space.

cards.question: What should you check after this section’s example?

blocks.text: A zombie is a process that has exited but whose termination status has not yet been collected by its parent. It is not continuing to execute application code or holding its former full address space.

Sending SIGKILL to a zombie does not solve the underlying problem because it has already exited. Investigate the parent and why it is not reaping children. A small transient number may be normal; a growing accumulation suggests a supervision or application defect.

Restarting a parent can be disruptive and should follow the service’s recovery procedure. Record the process relationship and growth pattern before acting. The visible zombie is evidence of a lifecycle problem, not an independent runaway workload.
Linux example — 7.14
Find zombie states without creating zombies deliberately.
ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,comm

topics.title: 7.15 Out-of-Memory Conditions
topics.summary: When memory cannot be supplied under the relevant constraints, the kernel or a userspace memory-pressure manager may terminate processes. A cgroup can encounter an out-of-memory condition even when the host still has free memory outside that group’s limit.

blocks.text: When memory cannot be supplied under the relevant constraints, the kernel or a userspace memory-pressure manager may terminate processes. A cgroup can encounter an out-of-memory condition even when the host still has free memory outside that group’s limit.

Inspect kernel logs, service logs, and cgroup memory events. Do not infer a global memory shortage solely from a service disappearing. Exit status, signal information, and recorded OOM evidence help distinguish causes.

Adding swap may provide breathing room for some workloads but can also introduce unacceptable latency. Increasing a limit without understanding growth can delay the same failure. The corrective action may be reducing concurrency, fixing a leak, changing caching behavior, or increasing capacity based on measured demand.

Search for OOM evidence on a systemd host.
sudo journalctl -k -b --no-pager

topics.title: 7.17 Control Groups
topics.summary: Control groups, or cgroups, organize processes for resource accounting and control. They can constrain CPU, memory, process counts, and I/O according to available controllers. systemd uses cgroups to group service processes and apply policy.

blocks.text: Control groups, or cgroups, organize processes for resource accounting and control. They can constrain CPU, memory, process counts, and I/O according to available controllers. systemd uses cgroups to group service processes and apply policy.

Cgroup v2 presents a unified hierarchy with controller-specific interfaces. A limit is meaningful only when the relevant controller and hierarchy support it. Do not blindly write values into /sys/fs/cgroup on a system managed by another owner.

Use systemd properties such as MemoryMax=, CPUQuota=, and TasksMax= for managed services when appropriate. A quota limits available CPU time; a weight influences relative competition. Neither is a substitute for understanding workload requirements. Test throttling and failure behavior before applying limits to production. (R16)
Linux example — 7.17
Inspect this process's cgroup placement.

cat /proc/$$/cgroup
findmnt -t cgroup,cgroup2

topics.title: Command walkthrough
topics.summary: Change — one ordinary-user process. Run in a single Bash session:

blocks.text: Change — one ordinary-user process. Run in a single Bash session:

sleep 120 &
pid=$!
printf 'created PID %s\n' "$pid"
ps -p "$pid" -o pid,ppid,user,stat,ni,etime,comm
kill -STOP "$pid"
ps -p "$pid" -o pid,stat,comm
kill -CONT "$pid"
kill -TERM "$pid"
wait "$pid"
status=$?
printf 'wait status=%s\n' "$status"

topics.title: Interpretation and recovery
topics.summary: There is no reason to use SIGKILL because sleep responds to termination. The parent shell collects the status with wait. Verify that the identified process is no longer present, but do not treat a later reused PID as the original task.

blocks.text: There is no reason to use SIGKILL because sleep responds to termination. The parent shell collects the status with wait. Verify that the identified process is no longer present, but do not treat a later reused PID as the original task.

For a real service, use the service manager to stop the whole managed unit. A PID captured by a script is useful within a controlled lifetime, not a permanent handle suitable for a future maintenance window.
